notes_cards.title: The Audition and the Compounding Machine

content.body_md:
Two ideas anchor this session — the internship as audition and the career as compounding machine — and understanding both shapes how you act in the near term and the long term.

**The internship is an audition, so perform from day one.** An internship's real purpose, from the firm's side, is *evaluation* — it's an extended, low-risk trial to assess whether you should get a permanent role. This means **everything you do during the internship is being judged as evidence for the conversion decision** — your work quality, your reliability, your attitude, your fit, your initiative. So the intern's job is to *perform from day one* as if the permanent offer depends on it (because it does) — to treat the internship as the live audition it is, not a relaxed settling-in period. The key implications:
- *Perform immediately.* Don't "settle in slowly" — the evaluation starts on day one, so perform from day one. Early impressions matter, and the whole period is being judged.
- *Deliver excellent work.* The single most important thing is the *quality of your work* — do excellent, reliable work that proves you'd be a valuable permanent hire. Your output is the core evidence in the conversion decision.
- *Show the right attitude and fit.* Beyond the work, demonstrate reliability, initiative, professionalism, and genuine fit with the team — because they're deciding whether they want *you* on the desk permanently, which is about character and fit as well as capability.
The intern who performs from day one, delivers excellent work, and shows the right attitude *converts* the audition into a PPO; the one who treats it as a relaxed stint converts nothing. The internship is an audition — act like it.

**Ownership is what converts (ship owned work, don't just "assist").** A specific, crucial principle for converting: the interns who convert are those who *own real work and ship it*, not those who merely "assist." There's a profound difference between an intern who *assists* (helps with others' work, does tasks as directed, contributes invisibly) and one who *owns a deliverable end to end* (takes responsibility for a real piece of work — a research note, an analysis, a model — and ships it, producing visible, attributable output). Ownership converts because it *proves you can do the actual job*: an intern who has independently produced a real, useful piece of research has demonstrated, concretely, that they'd be a productive permanent analyst — while an intern who only "assisted" has demonstrated little, because their contribution is invisible and unattributable. So the converting intern *seeks ownership* — volunteers to own a deliverable, takes a piece of work end to end, ships visible output — rather than passively assisting. Ship owned work, not just assistance, because owned work is the proof of capability that converts the audition.

**The career is a compounding machine, so build continuously.** Beyond the internship, the larger truth: **a career is a compounding asset, where the things you build — reputation, relationships, body of work, skills — accumulate and compound over decades, each paying dividends and enabling the next.** This means:
- *The assets you build keep paying.* Your reputation, once built, opens doors throughout your career; your relationships deepen and connect you to opportunities for decades; your body of work and track record accumulate into ever-greater credibility. What you build doesn't expire after the job search — it compounds.
- *Each asset enables the next.* A good early role (won via your assets) builds more reputation and relationships, which win a better next role, which builds more — the assets compound on each other, accelerating over a career. The early investment in building reputation, relationships, and a body of work pays *increasing* dividends over time.
- *So build deliberately and continuously.* Because the career compounds, the wise analyst *keeps building* the compounding assets throughout their career — continuing to build their reputation, deepen their relationships, grow their body of work, sharpen their skills — knowing it all compounds. The everything-you-built-in-this-module isn't a one-time job-search toolkit; it's the start of a *lifelong* compounding system, and continuing to build it is what makes a career accelerate.

**How they connect:** The internship (audition) and the career (compounding machine) connect through *everything you've built in this module.* You use your assets (proof-of-work, reputation, network) to *win* the internship/role; you *convert* the internship by performing and shipping owned work (which itself builds more reputation and relationships — compounding assets); and you *keep building* those assets throughout your career, where they compound for decades. The deepest point: **the internship is the near-term audition where your assets convert into a permanent seat, and the career is the long-term compounding machine where those assets keep paying dividends — so perform from day one to convert the audition, and build continuously to compound the career**, because everything you've built in this module is a compounding asset that, treated this way, keeps working for you for decades. Break in by treating the internship as the audition it is; build a great career by treating it as the compounding machine it is.

🧠 Remember: Two anchoring ideas — the internship is an audition (everything is judged for the conversion decision, so perform from day one, deliver excellent work, show the right attitude, and crucially *ship owned work* rather than just assisting, because owned work proves you can do the job and is what converts), and the career is a compounding machine (reputation, relationships, and body of work accumulate and compound over decades, each enabling the next, so build deliberately and continuously) — connected because your assets win the role, convert the internship, and keep compounding for a lifetime.

notes_cards.title: Converting the Internship and Compounding the Career

content.body_md:
Let me give you the concrete playbook for both — how to actually convert an internship into a PPO, and how to build the compounding career — so this closing session leaves you with actionable approaches for the near term and the long term.

**CONVERTING THE INTERNSHIP — the audition playbook:**

- *Perform from day one.* Treat the internship as a live evaluation from the first day — bring energy, focus, and your best work immediately, not after a settling-in period. The conversion decision is informed by the *whole* internship, including the start, so make every week count.
- *Deliver excellent, reliable work.* Make the quality and reliability of your work your top priority — do everything you're given excellently, meet every deadline, be someone the team can depend on. Your work is the core evidence in the conversion decision, so make it consistently excellent. Reliability matters as much as brilliance — be someone they can count on.
- *Seek and ship owned work.* This is the conversion lever: don't just assist — *seek ownership* of real deliverables. Volunteer to own a piece of work (a research note, an analysis, a model), take it end to end, and *ship* a useful, attributable output. An intern who has independently produced a real, valuable piece of research has proven they can do the job — the strongest possible conversion evidence. Look for opportunities to own and ship visible work, and deliver it excellently.
- *Go beyond the brief.* The interns who stand out *exceed* expectations — delivering not just what was asked but a bit more (the extra analysis, the cleaner output, the useful insight no one requested). Going beyond the brief signals initiative and the ownership mindset that mark a strong permanent hire (it's exactly the "delivered beyond what was asked" quality that distinguishes the converting intern). Look for ways to add value beyond your assigned tasks.
- *Build relationships and fit.* Convert the *people* too — build genuine relationships with the team (the give-first philosophy, applied internally), demonstrate you're someone they'd want on the desk (professional, collaborative, genuine), and become someone the team *advocates* for in the conversion decision. Fit and relationships matter alongside the work.
- *Follow up and stay engaged — never go silent.* Toward the end and after, *follow up specifically and stay in touch* — never just disappear. A specific, genuine follow-up (on your work, your interest, the opportunity) keeps you top of mind for the conversion decision; going silent forfeits the momentum. And if a PPO doesn't come immediately, staying genuinely in touch keeps the relationship (and future opportunities) alive. Never go silent — specific follow-up and continued engagement are what keep the conversion (and the relationship) alive.

**COMPOUNDING THE CAREER — the long game:**

- *Keep building your reputation.* Don't stop building your reputation once you've broken in — keep publishing, keep doing visible good work, keep growing your standing in the field (the LinkedIn/content arc, continued). Your reputation compounds over a career, opening ever-greater doors, so keep investing in it.
- *Keep deepening and growing your network.* Continue building genuine relationships (the give-first philosophy, for life) — deepening existing relationships and building new ones throughout your career. Your network compounds — relationships deepen, connect you to opportunities, and multiply over decades — so keep investing in genuine relationships, always give-first.
- *Keep building your body of work and track record.* Keep accumulating a body of excellent work and a strong track record — each piece adding to your credibility, each success enabling the next. Your body of work and track record compound into ever-greater credibility and opportunity, so keep building them.
- *Keep sharpening your skills and expertise.* Keep learning and deepening your expertise (continued mastery — the whole course, for a career) — because your skills and expertise compound into greater capability and value over time. Never stop building your craft.
- *Let each role build the assets that win the next.* Approach each role as both valuable in itself and as a *builder* of the compounding assets (reputation, relationships, body of work, skills) that win the next, better role. The career compounds when each step deliberately builds the assets for the next — so always be building, knowing it compounds.

**THE INTEGRATED CLOSE:** Put together, this is how everything you've built keeps working: you *win* the internship/role using your assets (the whole module); you *convert* the internship by performing from day one, delivering excellent work, shipping owned work, exceeding the brief, building relationships, and following up — turning the audition into a PPO; and you *compound* the career by continuing to build your reputation, network, body of work, and skills throughout your career, where they pay dividends for decades. The internship is the near-term conversion of your assets into a permanent seat; the compounding career is the long-term truth that your assets keep paying. And the through-line of the entire module is this: the positioning, proof-of-work, reputation, influence, and relationships you've learned to build are *compounding assets* — not one-time tools, but the foundation of a career that keeps building itself. Treat the internship as the audition it is and the career as the compounding machine it is, and you don't just break into equity research — you build a career, on a foundation of deliberately-built and continuously-compounding assets, that keeps paying dividends for decades. That's the destination of this module: not just a first job, but a compounding career, built on assets you control and keep building. (A grounding note: converting an internship and compounding a career both rest on *genuine excellence and genuine relationships* — real, valuable work and real, give-first relationships, sustained over time; there are no shortcuts, but the compounding rewards the genuine, continuous building richly.)

🧠 Remember: Convert the internship with the audition playbook — perform from day one, deliver excellent reliable work, *seek and ship owned work* (the conversion lever), go beyond the brief, build relationships and fit, and follow up specifically (never go silent) — and compound the career with the long game — keep building your reputation, network, body of work, and skills, letting each role build the assets that win the next — because the internship converts your assets into a permanent seat and the career compounds them for decades, so everything you've built keeps working for you.

notes_cards.title: Treating the Internship as a Line on the CV (and the Career as Job-to-Job)

content.body_md:
The error: two connected failures. In the near term, treating the *internship* as a relaxed stint or just a line on the CV — settling in slowly, doing only what's asked, "assisting" rather than owning, going silent afterward — squandering the audition. In the long term, treating the *career* as a series of separate jobs — building no compounding assets, thinking transactionally job-to-job, starting from scratch each time — forfeiting the compounding.

Why it happens: the *internship* error happens because an internship doesn't *feel* like an interview (it's longer, more relaxed, framed as "experience"), so interns don't bring the urgency of an audition — they settle in, do the assigned tasks, and treat it as a line for the CV rather than a live evaluation. The *career* error happens because each job feels like a discrete thing, and the compounding nature of a career (assets built early paying dividends for decades) isn't obvious in the moment — so people think job-to-job, not realising they're forfeiting compounding. Both stem from not seeing the larger frame (audition; compounding machine).

The truth: **the internship is an audition where everything is judged (so a relaxed, assist-only, go-silent approach squanders the conversion), and the career is a compounding machine (so a job-to-job, build-nothing approach forfeits decades of compounding dividends).** On the internship: treating it as a relaxed CV-line means failing to perform when performance is being judged for the permanent offer — the relaxed intern who only assists and goes silent gives the firm little evidence to convert them, and converts nothing, while the intern who performs from day one and ships owned work converts. On the career: treating it as separate jobs means building no compounding assets (reputation, relationships, body of work) and starting from scratch each time — forfeiting the compounding that makes careers accelerate, while the analyst who builds continuously compounds for decades. Both errors come from not acting on the larger frame: the internship *is* an audition (so perform), and the career *is* a compounding machine (so build continuously).

The consequence: the intern who treats it as a CV line squanders one of the most powerful conversion opportunities in a career (a relaxed, assist-only internship rarely converts to a PPO), and the analyst who thinks job-to-job forfeits the compounding that would have made their career accelerate (starting from scratch each time, while peers who built continuously pull ahead). The fix is to act on both frames: treat the internship as the *audition* it is (perform from day one, deliver excellent work, ship owned work, exceed the brief, build relationships, follow up — convert it), and treat the career as the *compounding machine* it is (keep building reputation, relationships, body of work, and skills throughout, letting them compound for decades). Don't waste the audition by treating it as a relaxed CV line; don't forfeit the compounding by thinking job-to-job. The internship converts your assets into a seat *if* you treat it as an audition; the career compounds your assets for decades *if* you keep building them. See both frames, act on both, and everything you've built keeps working — squander either, and you leave enormous value on the table. Treat the internship as the audition and the career as the compounding machine.

🧠 Remember: Don't treat the internship as a relaxed CV line (it's an audition where everything is judged for the conversion, so settling in slowly, assisting rather than owning, and going silent squanders one of the most powerful conversion opportunities) and don't treat the career as job-to-job (it's a compounding machine, so building no compounding assets forfeits decades of accelerating dividends); act on both frames — perform from day one and ship owned work to convert the audition, and build reputation, relationships, body of work, and skills continuously to compound the career — because that's how everything you've built keeps working for you.

notes_cards.title: The Intern Who Owned a Research Note — and the Career That Compounded

content.body_md:
Let me close with the pattern that ties the whole module together — an intern who converted through ownership, and whose career then compounded on the assets they kept building — because it shows both reframes in action and how everything in this module keeps paying off.

**The conversion through ownership.** Two interns join the same equity research desk for a three-month internship. The *first* treats it as a relaxed stint and a CV line — settling in slowly, doing the tasks assigned, "assisting" senior analysts with their work, contributing invisibly, and at the end simply leaving, assuming the internship would speak for itself. They did nothing *wrong*, but they gave the firm little concrete evidence that they'd be a valuable permanent analyst — their contribution was invisible and unattributable, mere assistance. So no PPO came; the internship was a line on their CV and nothing more. The *second* intern treated it as the *audition* it was. From day one, they performed — excellent, reliable work on everything assigned. And crucially, they *sought ownership*: they volunteered to own a real deliverable — an independent research note on a company — took it end to end, and *shipped* a genuinely useful, clean, attributable piece of analysis (applying everything from the course — the analysis, the writing, the rigour). They went beyond the brief, built genuine relationships with the team, and followed up specifically about their interest and their work. By the end, the firm had concrete, attributable evidence that this intern could do the actual job — they'd *shipped real, valuable research* — and the team, who'd come to know and rate them, advocated for them. The second intern converted: a PPO, a permanent seat. The difference was *ownership* — shipping owned work that proved capability, versus invisible assistance that proved little.

**The career that compounded.** Now extend the second intern's story over years — because the conversion was just the start of a *compounding* career. Having broken in, they kept building the compounding assets (the long game). They kept building their *reputation* — continuing to publish and do visible good work, growing their standing. They kept deepening their *network* — maintaining and growing genuine give-first relationships throughout the industry. They kept accumulating a *body of work and track record* — each excellent analysis adding to their credibility. They kept sharpening their *skills and expertise* — deepening their mastery. And these assets *compounded*: their growing reputation and relationships won them a better next role; that role built more reputation and relationships, winning a better one after that; their body of work and credibility accumulated into ever-greater opportunity. Each asset enabled the next, and the career *accelerated* — because they treated it as the compounding machine it is, building deliberately and continuously, while peers who thought job-to-job started from scratch each time and fell behind. Over a decade, the compounding produced a career far greater than any single job — built on the assets they'd kept building since the start.

The lesson ties the whole module together: **the intern converted by treating the internship as an audition and shipping owned work (the proof of capability that converts), and the career compounded by treating it as a compounding machine and continuously building the assets (reputation, relationships, body of work, skills) that pay dividends for decades.** The first intern squandered the audition (relaxed, assist-only) and converted nothing; the second converted through ownership and then compounded through continuous building. And the through-line is *everything this module taught*: the positioning, proof-of-work, reputation, influence, and relationships are *compounding assets* — they won the internship, the owned work that converted it drew on them, and continuing to build them compounded the career for decades. This is the destination of the entire module: not just breaking in, but building a compounding career on deliberately-built assets you control and keep building. Treat the internship as the audition (perform, ship owned work, convert) and the career as the compounding machine (build continuously, compound for decades), and everything you've built keeps working for you — for a career, not just a first job. That's the payoff of the whole journey. (Illustrative composite of a real and repeated pattern — the principle is that ownership converts internships and that careers compound on continuously-built assets, the destination of everything this module teaches.)

🧠 Remember: The intern who converted treated the internship as an audition and *shipped owned work* — an independent research note, end to end — proving capability where the assist-only intern proved little, and then the career *compounded* as they kept building reputation, relationships, body of work, and skills, each asset winning a better role and enabling the next, accelerating over a decade; the through-line is that everything this module taught is a compounding asset that wins the internship, converts it through owned work, and compounds the career for decades — the destination of the whole journey.

project.title: Build Your Equity Research Career System
todo_list: **Define your positioning** (Session 14.1): choose a precise target (sell-side vs buy-side, sector lean, firm style), define the specific analyst-identity you'll occupy ("someone already producing like an analyst..."), list your proof points, and name your differentiation — write it as a one-paragraph positioning statement that everything else will reinforce.

**Build your world-class ER resume** (Sessions 14.2–14.3): architect it to win all three judges — clean parseable formatting and genuine ER keywords (the ATS), strongest material high and scannable (the skim), and a structure that leads the analyst to your evidence (the close read); write every bullet at the achievement level, and *every research bullet at the analytical level* (thesis + drivers + risk + judgement); open with a positioning summary. Remove every duty-only line.

**Build your proof-of-work portfolio** (Session 14.4): produce (or polish) at least one — ideally two or three — *deep, genuinely-rigorous* full equity research analyses (model + defensible thesis) on real NSE companies in your target sectors, plus a plan for a regular stream of shorter pieces; make it tangible, and you must be able to defend every thesis and number.

**Engineer your LinkedIn profile** (Session 14.5): optimise the high-weight fields with genuine ER keywords (found in search) and build a converting profile — a sharp positioning headline ("[role] | [specialty] | [proof]"), a persuasive first-person About, your best research pinned in Featured, and analytical Experience/Projects/Skills; complete every section.

**Build and launch your content engine** (Sessions 14.6–14.7): plan your content mix (the credibility core of original analysis, plus reach drivers and relatability builders), all reinforcing your positioning/niche; write and publish at least three pieces, each crafted to land (a strong hook, scannable structure, a high-reach format like a carousel for analysis); commit to a sustainable cadence.

**Choose your niche and influence path** (Session 14.8): name the specific niche you'll build authority in (aligned to your positioning), and outline your plan to become a recognised voice in it (consistent niche content, genuine community engagement) — building toward inbound opportunity.

**Identify your top-tier targets** (Sessions 14.9–14.10): identify ~10 specific genuinely-senior people aligned to your targets — senior analysts, PMs, research heads at or connected to your target firms — and genuinely research each one's actual work.

**Build your give-first outreach** (Sessions 14.9–14.10): for three of them, plan and write *specific, genuine, give-first* outreach — preceded by genuine public engagement with their work, leading with value (a thoughtful insight, your own relevant analysis), with no or a tiny easy ask — that cuts through the generic flood; map how you'll build each relationship over time, give-first.

**Plan your referral system** (Session 14.11): map how you'll *earn* referrals (build genuine relationships demonstrating your capability and reliability over time) and how you'll make the ask easy when the moment is right (prepare a CV and a ready-to-paste referral blurb); never plan a cold referral ask to a stranger.

**Plan your internship conversion and compounding** (Session 14.12): outline how you'd convert an internship into a PPO (perform from day one, ship owned work, follow up) and how you'll keep building your compounding assets (reputation, network, body of work, skills) over your career.

**Align everything to your positioning** (Session 14.1): review the whole system and ensure every element — resume, portfolio, profile, content, outreach — reinforces the *one* identity from your positioning statement; fix anything scattered or off-message.
**Track and refine** your outreach and content (response rates, engagement) in a simple sheet, refining what underperforms.

**Everything is aligned to one clear positioning — it's a system, not scattered tactics.** The standout submission reads as a *coherent whole*: the positioning statement is sharp and specific, and the resume, portfolio, profile, content, and outreach *all visibly reinforce the same analyst-identity*. A reviewer encountering any element gets the same compelling, consistent message — which is exactly what makes a candidacy memorable and winning, versus a pile of disconnected, generic tactics.

**The resume wins all three judges, and every research bullet is analytical.** A great resume is clean and parseable (clears the ATS), scannable with strong material high (survives the skim), and — decisively — rewards the analyst's close read with genuine evidence of an analytical mind: every bullet at least an achievement, and every *research* bullet at the analytical level (thesis + drivers + risk + judgement). Not a single duty-only line survives, and the resume reads like the work of someone who already thinks like an analyst.

**The proof-of-work is real, deep, and defensible.** The portfolio contains at least one *genuinely rigorous* full analysis on a real company (model + defensible thesis + real drivers + acknowledged risks + primary sources + clear writing) — work the candidate could confidently defend in an interview, not a hollow template-fill. This is the asset that makes the candidacy undeniable, and its depth and genuineness are what a hiring analyst would respect.

**The networking is genuinely give-first and reaches genuinely senior people — no cold asks anywhere.** The standout outreach targets *genuinely senior* people (senior analysts, PMs, research heads), is built on *real research and engagement* with each person's actual work, leads with *value* (specific, genuine, give-first), and contains *no cold ask* — and the referral plan *earns* referrals through relationship and trust rather than asking strangers. There is no "please refer me" to a near-stranger anywhere; every approach reflects the give-first philosophy that reaches and wins top-tier people.

**It's built as a compounding career asset, not a one-time toolkit.** The best submissions treat the system as the *start* of a compounding career — the LinkedIn presence built toward genuine influence in a niche, the relationships built genuinely to deepen over time, the proof-of-work as a growing body, the whole thing designed to keep building and compounding. The candidate demonstrates they understand that positioning, proof-of-work, reputation, influence, and relationships are *compounding assets* they'll keep building for a career — so the system isn't just aimed at a first job, but at a career that keeps building itself.

capstones.title: Initiating Coverage: The Full Equity Research Report

meta.Prerequisites: Financial Modelling · FSA · Forensic/Red-Flag Accounting · Advanced Ratio Analysis · Valuation · Annual Report Reading
meta.Tools: Excel/Sheets · NSE/BSE filings · Screener/Tijori/vendor data · concall transcripts
meta.Output: A publication-grade initiating-coverage report (15–25 pages) + 1-page tear sheet + the underlying model

capstones.brief: Produce a full institutional **initiating coverage report** on one NSE-listed company a buy-side PM would actually act on. The bar is not "did you build a DCF" — it is "does your thesis contain a *variant perception* the Street doesn't already hold, defended by a model with no plugs and a forensic check that proves the numbers are real."
capstones.learning_outcomes: By the end, the student can: build a driver-based 3-statement model from filings; construct a DCF with a defensible Indian WACC; triangulate value across methods; run a forensic quality-of-earnings review; articulate a non-consensus thesis with catalysts and risks; and write to institutional standard.
capstones.final_deliverables:
1. The initiating coverage report (structure specified below)
2. The 1-page tear sheet
3. The full Excel model (3-statement + DCF + comps + scenarios)
4. The forensic earnings-quality scorecard
5. Viva defence (20 min)
capstones.required_structure:
The report **must** contain these sections, in this order. This is the blueprint of the "full long equity research report":

1. **Cover block** — rating, 12-month target price, CMP, implied upside/downside, market cap, key trading data, one-line thesis
2. **Investment summary** — the thesis in 4–6 tight paragraphs
3. **The variant perception** — where and why your view diverges from consensus, and the catalyst that closes the gap
4. **Business overview** — model teardown, revenue architecture, unit economics, the moat *with evidence*
5. **Industry & competitive landscape** — structure (Porter's), TAM/SAM/SOM, regulatory regime, value-chain position
6. **Financial analysis** — 5-year historical performance, segment trends, margin bridge, capital allocation, returns (ROE/ROIC vs cost of capital)
7. **Earnings quality / forensic review** — the scorecard and its narrative
8. **Valuation** — DCF (assumptions + WACC build), relative valuation (normalised comps), and the football field
9. **Scenario analysis** — bull / base / bear with explicit driver assumptions and resulting targets
10. **Investment risks** — each paired with a mitigant and a leading indicator
11. **Catalysts & triggers** — dated calendar
12. **Management & governance** — promoter behaviour, board quality, related-party/pledge analysis, capital-allocation track record
13. **Financial summary tables** — P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, ratio sheet (3 years history + 3 years forecast)
14. **Appendices** — full model assumptions, peer comp table, channel-check notes, glossary
capstones.tasks_raw:
**Task 1.1 — Universe screen & company selection**
- **Objective:** Pick a name where a differentiated view is actually findable.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Screen NSE for companies ₹5,000–50,000 Cr mkt cap (under-covered band)
  - [ ] Filter for adequate disclosure, ≥5 years of filings, and a live debate (bull/bear tension)
  - [ ] Shortlist 3 names; pick 1 and document why
- **Produce:** A short selection rationale (½ page).
- **Done when:** The company is in the target cap band, has 5+ years of data, and you can name the consensus you intend to challenge.

**Task 1.2 — Thesis memo (the variant perception)**
- **Objective:** Commit to a call before the model can bias you.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Pull Street estimates / consensus rating where available
  - [ ] State your call (Buy/Hold/Sell) and the *one thing the market is missing*
  - [ ] List the 3 pillars supporting it and the 1 fact that would falsify it
- **Produce:** A one-page thesis memo.
- **Done when:** The memo names a *specific* divergence from consensus, not a restatement of it.

**Task 1.3 — Business model teardown**
- **Objective:** Understand how the company actually makes money.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Map revenue architecture (segments × volume × price × mix)
  - [ ] Define unit economics and the cost structure (fixed vs variable)
  - [ ] Identify the moat and *prove it* (pricing power, switching costs, cost curve, network) with evidence
- **Produce:** Section 4 of the report.
- **Done when:** The moat claim is backed by data (margins vs peers, churn, pricing history), not adjectives.

**Task 1.4 — Industry & competitive analysis**
- **Objective:** Place the company in its structural context.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Porter's five forces with India specifics
  - [ ] TAM/SAM/SOM build with sourced numbers
  - [ ] Map the regulatory regime (SEBI + sector regulator) and value-chain position
  - [ ] Benchmark the company vs 3–5 peers on growth, margins, returns
- **Produce:** Section 5.
- **Done when:** You can state the company's relative position and why it's defensible or fragile.

**Task 1.5 — Forensic / quality-of-earnings scorecard**
- **Objective:** Confirm the reported numbers are economically real before you forecast them.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Accruals analysis + 5-year CFO vs PAT conversion
  - [ ] Revenue-recognition quality, capitalised-vs-expensed choices
  - [ ] Related-party transactions, contingent liabilities, promoter pledge trajectory, auditor history
  - [ ] Compute the **Beneish M-score**
- **Produce:** A one-page green/amber/red **earnings-quality scorecard** + Section 7 narrative.
- **Done when:** Every red/amber flag is sourced to a filing page and explained.

**Task 1.6 — Historical financial spreading**
- **Objective:** Build the clean historical base for the model.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Spread 5 years of P&L, balance sheet, cash flow from filings
  - [ ] Normalise for one-offs; apply Ind AS adjustments (e.g. Ind AS 116 leases)
  - [ ] Build the historical ratio sheet (growth, margins, returns, leverage, working capital)
- **Produce:** Historical sheets in the model + Section 6.
- **Done when:** Historicals tie to audited filings to the rupee and one-offs are flagged.

**Task 1.7 — Driver-based revenue model**
- **Objective:** Forecast revenue from operating drivers, never a single growth %.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build segment-level drivers (volume, price, mix, capacity, utilisation)
  - [ ] Tie drivers to industry/competitive assumptions from Task 1.4
  - [ ] Document every assumption with its rationale
- **Produce:** The revenue build in the model.
- **Done when:** Revenue is explained by drivers a reviewer can challenge, each with a stated basis.

**Task 1.8 — Full 3-statement model**
- **Objective:** A fully integrated, internally consistent model.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build the integrated P&L → balance sheet → cash flow with working-capital and debt schedules
  - [ ] Ensure the balance sheet balances every period with **no plugs**
  - [ ] Forecast 3–5 years, quarterly and annual
- **Produce:** The core model.
- **Done when:** The three statements articulate, the BS balances every period, and circularity (if any) is controlled.

**Task 1.9 — DCF valuation & WACC**
- **Objective:** An intrinsic value with a defensible discount rate.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build FCFF, explicit horizon + terminal value via *both* Gordon growth and exit multiple
  - [ ] Construct WACC (Indian risk-free, ERP, levered/unlevered beta, cost of debt, capital weights)
  - [ ] Reconcile the two terminal-value methods
- **Produce:** Part of Section 8.
- **Done when:** Each WACC input is sourced and the terminal value isn't doing all the work unexplained.

**Task 1.10 — Relative valuation & football field**
- **Objective:** Cross-check intrinsic value against the market.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build a normalised peer-comp table (EV/EBITDA, P/E, P/B, growth-adjusted)
  - [ ] Adjust for accounting/capital-structure differences
  - [ ] Build a **football field** reconciling DCF, comps, and any SOTP
- **Produce:** Rest of Section 8.
- **Done when:** The football field reconciles methods and your target price sits inside a defensible range.

**Task 1.11 — Scenario analysis & sensitivities**
- **Objective:** Show the distribution of outcomes, not a point estimate.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build bull / base / bear with *explicit* driver assumptions (not ±10%)
  - [ ] Sensitivity tables: WACC × terminal growth; key operating driver × exit multiple
  - [ ] Assign rough probabilities and an expected value
- **Produce:** Section 9.
- **Done when:** Each scenario is driver-defined and the target reflects probability-weighted thinking.

**Task 1.12 — Risk, catalysts & governance**
- **Objective:** Frame what could go wrong and what forces the re-rating.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] List key risks, each with a mitigant and a leading indicator
  - [ ] Build a dated catalyst calendar (results, regulatory events, capital-allocation events)
  - [ ] Assess management/governance: pledge, RPT, board quality, capital-allocation record
- **Produce:** Sections 10–12.
- **Done when:** Risks are specific and monitorable; catalysts are dated.

**Task 1.13 — Primary / alternative research**
- **Objective:** Triangulate the desk research with the real world.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Run ≥2 channel checks (distributors, customers, ex-employees — scuttlebutt)
  - [ ] Pull ≥1 alt-data proxy (hiring, GST/EPFO, web traffic, footfall)
  - [ ] Reconcile findings against the model; adjust if warranted
- **Produce:** Appendix channel-check notes.
- **Done when:** At least one model assumption is confirmed or revised by primary evidence.

**Task 1.14 — Write the report**
- **Objective:** Assemble the long-form initiation to institutional standard.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Write all 14 sections in the required structure
  - [ ] Lead with the thesis and the variant perception; keep it PM-actionable
  - [ ] Insert the financial summary tables and football field charts
- **Produce:** The 15–25 page report.
- **Done when:** It reads like a real initiation: clear rating, target, differentiated view, and an analyst could trade off it.

**Task 1.15 — Tear sheet & viva**
- **Objective:** Distil and defend.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build a 1-page tear sheet (rating, target, thesis, key financials, risks)
  - [ ] Prepare for and pass a 20-minute viva where the panel attacks the thesis
- **Produce:** Tear sheet + viva.
- **Done when:** The tear sheet stands alone and you survive the panel's challenges.

### Evaluation rubric
| Criterion | Needs work | Good | Excellent |
|-----------|-----------|------|-----------|
| Thesis differentiation | Restates consensus | Mild tilt | Sharp, evidenced variant view + catalyst |
| Model integrity | Plugs, doesn't tie out | Growth-rate driven, ties out | Driver-based, no plugs, fully articulated |
| Forensic rigour | Surface ratios | Accruals + conversion | Full QoE scorecard, M-score, RPT/pledge |
| Valuation | One method | DCF + comps | Triangulated, defensible WACC, football field |
| Communication | Data dump | Clear structure | Reads like a real initiation; PM-actionable |

### Stretch goals
- Initiate on a *basket* of 3 names in one sub-sector with relative rankings
- Build the model to auto-refresh from the latest filing

capstones.title: Sector Coverage & Comparative Stock Ranking

meta.Prerequisites: CAP-01 · FSA · Advanced Ratio Analysis · Sector Analysis · Valuation
meta.Tools: Excel/Sheets · NSE/BSE filings · vendor data · concall transcripts
meta.Output: A sector coverage note (8–12 pages) ranking 4–6 peers, with a Top Pick and a Least Preferred call

capstones.brief: Cover a single sector the way a junior sell-side analyst does on day one: analyse the structure, benchmark 4–6 listed peers side by side, and produce a **ranked comparative note** with a clearly argued Top Pick and Least Preferred. This is deliberately *breadth over depth* — you're not building a full model on each name (CAP-01 already proved you can). You're proving you can compare companies fairly, rank them on a defensible framework, and form a relative view. That relative skill is the core of sector coverage.
capstones.learning_outcomes: The student can: analyse a sector's structure and demand drivers; build a clean comparative financials sheet across peers; normalise for accounting differences; apply relative valuation; design a transparent scoring/ranking framework; and defend a "prefer A over B" call.
capstones.final_deliverables:
1. The sector coverage note (structure below)
2. The comparative financials & valuation sheet (the "comp sheet")
3. The ranking scorecard
4. Viva defence (15 min)
capstones.required_structure:
1. **Sector snapshot** — size, growth, structure, key demand drivers, regulatory backdrop
2. **Where we are in the cycle** — the current setup and the near-term outlook
3. **The peer set** — who's in it and why, with a one-line positioning of each
4. **Comparative financials** — growth, margins, returns (ROE/ROIC), leverage, working-capital efficiency, side by side
5. **Comparative valuation** — relative multiples, normalised; cheap vs expensive *and why*
6. **The ranking** — the scoring framework and the resulting order
7. **Top Pick & Least Preferred** — the two calls, argued
8. **Key sector risks** — what would change the whole view
9. **Appendix** — the comp sheet, sources
capstones.tasks_raw:
**Task 2.1 — Sector selection & structure**
- **Objective:** Choose a sector and map how it works.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Pick a coverable Indian sector (e.g. IT services, private banks, cement, FMCG, autos, hospitals)
  - [ ] Map size, growth, demand drivers, regulatory backdrop, and the basic competitive structure
  - [ ] State where the sector sits in its cycle right now
- **Produce:** Sections 1–2 of the note.
- **Done when:** A reader understands what moves this sector and the current setup, with sourced numbers.

**Task 2.2 — Peer set & positioning**
- **Objective:** Define a fair, comparable peer set.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Select 4–6 listed peers that are genuinely comparable
  - [ ] Write a one-line positioning for each (what kind of player it is)
  - [ ] Note any that aren't strictly comparable and how you'll adjust
- **Produce:** Section 3.
- **Done when:** The peer set is defensible and each name's role in the sector is clear.

**Task 2.3 — Comparative financials (the comp sheet)**
- **Objective:** Benchmark the peers on the same metrics, fairly.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Pull 3–5 years of key financials for each peer
  - [ ] Build a side-by-side sheet: revenue growth, margins, ROE/ROIC, leverage, working-capital cycle, cash conversion
  - [ ] Normalise for obvious accounting/one-off differences so the comparison is apples-to-apples
- **Produce:** The comp sheet + Section 4.
- **Done when:** Every peer is measured on the same, normalised basis and the differences are visible at a glance.

**Task 2.4 — Comparative valuation**
- **Objective:** Establish who's cheap, who's expensive, and why.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build relative multiples (P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/B as relevant), normalised
  - [ ] Relate each multiple to the company's growth and returns (is the premium/discount deserved?)
  - [ ] Flag any genuine mispricing
- **Produce:** Section 5.
- **Done when:** Valuation gaps are explained by fundamentals, not just listed.

**Task 2.5 — Ranking framework & scorecard**
- **Objective:** Turn the analysis into a transparent ranking.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Design a scoring framework (e.g. growth, profitability/returns, balance-sheet strength, valuation, with stated weights)
  - [ ] Score each peer and produce the ranked order
  - [ ] Sense-check: does the ranking match the intuition from Tasks 2.3–2.4?
- **Produce:** The ranking scorecard + Section 6.
- **Done when:** The framework is explicit, the weights are justified, and the ranking is reproducible.

**Task 2.6 — Top Pick, Least Preferred & write-up**
- **Objective:** Form and defend the relative calls, then assemble the note.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Argue the Top Pick and the Least Preferred from the ranking
  - [ ] Write the sector risks that could change the whole view
  - [ ] Assemble the 8–12 page note in the required structure and defend it in a 15-min viva
- **Produce:** Sections 7–8 + the full note + viva.
- **Done when:** The two calls follow logically from the framework and survive the panel's "why not the other one?" challenge.

### Evaluation rubric
| Criterion | Needs work | Good | Excellent |
|-----------|-----------|------|-----------|
| Sector understanding | Generic overview | Solid structure & drivers | Sharp read on structure *and* the current cycle |
| Comparability | Inconsistent metrics | Same metrics | Normalised, genuinely apples-to-apples |
| Valuation reasoning | Lists multiples | Links to fundamentals | Explains every premium/discount, flags mispricing |
| Ranking framework | Opaque/arbitrary | Transparent | Transparent, weighted, reproducible, sense-checked |
| The calls | Unsupported | Reasoned | Clearly follow the framework; survive challenge |

### Stretch goals
- Add a light DCF on just the Top Pick to support the relative call
- Track the ranking's relative performance over the course duration

capstones.title: AI Equity Research Copilot

meta.Prerequisites: CAP-01 · AI & Prompt Engineering · FSA · Annual Report Reading
meta.Tools: An LLM API · a simple front-end (or notebook) · concall transcripts + results filings
meta.Output: A working AI tool that turns a concall + results into a structured, cited analyst note + a short build write-up

capstones.brief: Build a focused, well-engineered **AI research copilot**: feed it a company's latest concall transcript and results filing, and it produces a structured analyst note — key takeaways, guidance changes, management tone, red flags, and valuation context — every claim **cited** back to the source. This is the AI capstone, but deliberately scoped: a single-company analyst assistant done *well*, not a multi-month backtested quant platform. The skill on display is real LLM engineering (structured outputs, citations, guardrails) fused with knowing *what actually matters* in a concall — exactly the AI-plus-finance hybrid recruiters want, and it doubles as a filmable product demo.
capstones.learning_outcomes: The student can: design a multi-stage LLM pipeline with structured (JSON-schema) outputs; enforce citations and guard against hallucination; encode finance domain judgement into prompts (what's a red flag, what's a guidance change that matters); and evaluate an AI tool's output against a human analyst's read.
capstones.final_deliverables:
1. The working tool (UI or notebook) that produces the note
2. Sample outputs for ≥3 companies
3. A short evaluation comparing the tool's output to a human read
4. A build write-up (architecture + prompt design + limitations)
5. Demo + viva (15 min)
capstones.tasks_raw:
**Task 3.1 — Scope & output spec**
- **Objective:** Lock what the tool does before building it.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Define the inputs (concall transcript + results filing) and the 7-part output spec above
  - [ ] Define the JSON schema each section must conform to
  - [ ] Pick 3 test companies with available transcripts + filings
- **Produce:** A one-page spec + the JSON schema.
- **Done when:** The output contract and schema are fully specified before any prompting.

**Task 3.2 — Ingestion**
- **Objective:** Get the source documents into the pipeline cleanly.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build ingestion for the transcript and the results filing (chunk if needed)
  - [ ] Preserve location info (line/section/page) so citations can point back
- **Produce:** The ingestion step.
- **Done when:** Source text is loaded and each chunk retains a referenceable location.

**Task 3.3 — Structured extraction prompts**
- **Objective:** Produce the takeaways, guidance deltas, tone, and red flags as structured output.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Write versioned prompts for each output section, returning schema-valid JSON
  - [ ] Encode finance judgement: what counts as a guidance change, a tone shift, a red flag
  - [ ] Require a citation field on every extracted claim
- **Produce:** The extraction prompts + JSON outputs.
- **Done when:** Each section returns valid JSON with citations, and the judgement is encoded in the prompt, not left to chance.

**Task 3.4 — Numbers & valuation context layer**
- **Objective:** Ground the qualitative read in the actual figures.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Extract/insert the key reported numbers with YoY/QoQ context
  - [ ] Add a simple valuation-context section (multiples vs the stock's own history)
  - [ ] Cross-check that the narrative matches the numbers (flag if it doesn't)
- **Produce:** The numbers + valuation sections of the note.
- **Done when:** The note ties the management story to the reported figures and flags any mismatch.

**Task 3.5 — Guardrails & hallucination control**
- **Objective:** Make the tool trustworthy.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Enforce "cite or omit" — no claim without a source reference
  - [ ] Add a check that flags/strips any claim that can't be grounded in the input
  - [ ] Handle missing data gracefully (say "not disclosed" rather than inventing)
- **Produce:** The guardrail layer.
- **Done when:** The tool does not fabricate; ungrounded claims are caught.

**Task 3.6 — Evaluation vs a human read**
- **Objective:** Show the tool is actually good.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] For the 3 test companies, do your own quick human read of the concall
  - [ ] Compare the tool's takeaways/red flags to yours; note hits, misses, false positives
  - [ ] Summarise where it's reliable and where it isn't
- **Produce:** A short evaluation write-up.
- **Done when:** The tool's accuracy is assessed honestly against a human baseline.

**Task 3.7 — UI, write-up & demo**
- **Objective:** Package and defend.
- **Do:**
  - [ ] Build a simple UI (or clean notebook) that runs end-to-end and renders the note
  - [ ] Write the build write-up: architecture, prompt design, and honest limitations
  - [ ] Demo it live and defend the design choices in a 15-min viva
- **Produce:** The tool + write-up + demo.
- **Done when:** A stranger can run it on a new company and get a useful, cited note, and you can explain every design decision.

### Evaluation rubric
| Criterion | Needs work | Good | Excellent |
|-----------|-----------|------|-----------|
| LLM engineering | Single freeform prompt | Multi-stage, some structure | Multi-stage, schema-valid, versioned prompts |
| Citations & guardrails | Uncited, hallucinates | Mostly cited | "Cite or omit" enforced; fabrication caught |
| Finance judgement | Generic summary | Surfaces real takeaways | Encodes what *matters* (guidance, tone, red flags) |
| Numbers grounding | Qualitative only | Some figures | Narrative tied to numbers, mismatches flagged |
| Evaluation honesty | None | Informal check | Measured vs a human read, limitations stated |
| Usability | Brittle | Runs on test cases | Runs cleanly on a new company end-to-end |

### Stretch goals
- Add a second "critic" pass: a separate prompt that challenges the note's conclusions
- Support batch mode (a folder of transcripts → a folder of notes)
- Add a simple sentiment-trend view across a company's last few concalls
